title: Reverse Engineering An iPhone X Display
brief: The first part of my project to reverse engineer an iPhone X Display and control it from a microcontroller.
description:
Mobile displays are impressive pieces of technology. They can be a mere couple millimetres thick yet contain millions of densely packed pixels. In the iPhone X's case, the display is a 1125x2436 OLED panel.

# Goals and expectations My eventual goal in this project (which I have not obtained yet) is to be able to control an iPhone X display from a microcontroller. Given that the microcontroller I am targeting is the RP2350, there are some limitations to this project: - RP2350 does not have a MIPI DSI hardware peripheral. - In fact, no other microcontroller I know of has a MIPI DSI peripheral with the required 4 data lanes. - The display has 2,740,500 pixels, one frame therefore occupies 8 MB. RP2350 has just 512KB of ram so the displayed image must either be 1-bit (black and white) or be upscaled from a much lower resolution. - A semi-obvious remedy for the above might be to utilize an 8MB PSRAM chip, however the read/write speeds of the sort of chips compatible with RP2350 are not even close to what is required of a frame buffer. - It may be difficult to get the required bandwidth of 4.0 Gbps off of the microcontroller. Though, the theoretical maximum bandwidth of the RP2350 at 250MHz is 8Gbps, limited by DMA. As a result, realistically I will not be able to exploit the full capabilities of the display with just a microcontroller. My first task was learning all that I can about the iPhone X Display. I learned that it uses MIPI DSI as a base protocol (as do most mobile displays). Though I found out pretty quickly that there is not much public information, or community information on the iPhone X display. This is the information I gathered for the display: - Which connector is the display connection, and which is the touch connection - The pinout of the display connector (Shown later) - The protocol used to communicate with the display (MIPI DSI) - The display resolution (1125x2436) - The display mode used (almost certainly Video Mode) - The expected impedance of the MIPI link (90 ohm differential) ## The display connector My next task was analyzing the display connector.

The connector has 34 pins, most of which are either power pins, ground pins, or not connected to anything (pins prefixed with NC). The 10 MIPI pins are the ones we care about. These pins are prefixed with 90 to indicate they expect a 90-ohm differential impedance. This is very important because a change in impedance causes a reflection within the wire, adding to the distortion of the signal. The MIPI lines are high-speed and thus there are many ground (GND) connections placed in between the MIPI lines. This is done so that the path the current takes back from the display is close to the driving line. Current always flows in loops, so when current flows down a MIPI line, it must flow back through a GND line. Keeping the "loop" small reduces the inductance of the wire (how much of a magnetic field it creates) which reduces the impedance. ### Impedance I'd quickly like to touch on impedance. It's a complicated topic but roughly means the resistance that a wire has to the current induced by a sinusoidal voltage. It is not actual resistance, no energy is lost, but it does act like resistance in that it changes how the current in a wire moves relative to the voltage. The important thing for this project is that changes in impedance cause the reflection of signals. ## MIPI Wires MIPI DSI uses pairs of wires called differential pairs. Differential pairs are pairs of wires that are pulled to opposite voltages to send a signal. The idea is that if there is any interference, it will affect both wires and push them both higher or lower, while the **difference** (whether wire 1 is higher or lower than wire 2) remains constant. This resistance to interference allows them to run at extremely high frequencies, and at low voltages, which lowers energy usage. There is usually one clock pair, used to transmit a repeating clock signal, and 1 or more "data lanes" which are also differential pairs. The iPhone X display uses 4 data lanes and 1 clock lane, for a total of 10 wires. MIPI DSI has two modes, Low Power (LP) mode and High Speed (HS) mode. In LP mode, the clock lane is unused, and all but the first data lane are unused. The first data lane (data lane 0) is used as two individual wires, not as a differential pair. The clock is unused because the bits are encoded in transitions of the two Data Lane 0 wires, so a clock is not needed. LP mode typically has a speed of 10Mbps, or around 50ns per edge. High speed mode uses all data lanes and the clock lane, and the clock typically runs at 500MHz. The lanes all use Double Data Rate (DDR) though, which means that bits are transmitted on both clock edges, so the effective bandwidth per lane is doubled to 1Gbps. With 4 data lanes, this gives 4Gbps of bandwidth between the host (Phone) and the receiver (Display). ## Video Mode This display does not have any (much) internal memory, and so cannot store any actual image frames. This would be called a "frame buffer" if it had one, but this display lacks one likely to keep the display thin, simple and "dumb". As a result of having no frame buffer, pixels must be continuously streamed to the display because the individual OLED pixels can only retain their colour for a fraction of a second before losing it. Now the problems. Displays usually have "vendor commands" which are custom commands added to the display. These commands are usually not public and some of them may be used to set up the display and configure it. These commands are required to turn the display on. In order to properly interface with this display and to turn it on, I need to know exactly what commands are sent from the phone to the display. ## Logic Analyzers There are electrical tools called Logic Analyzers that record digital signals and allow you to look at and analyze them. This is exactly what I need, and there are many types of logic analyzers with different "sample rates". I believe the commands I will be needing to record are sent in LP mode, so at a minimum I will need a logic analyzer capable of reliably capturing a 10MHz signal. For that, I will need a logical analyzer with a sample rate at least 5x the edge rate (20MHz). ![logic-analyzer-output.png](/design-assets/images/7843876.webp) My first hurdle is realizing that a 100MHz+ analyzer cost **$225+** which is at least 10 sushi meals that I would rather enjoy putting in my belly. Since risking my sushi supply is out of the question, I'm going to need to make my own logic analyzer from what I have on hand, which is a Raspberry Pi Pico 2, containing the RP2350 microcontroller. I also need to connect the analyzer to the link between the phone and display without corrupting or damaging the signal. High speed signals are very delicate, and connecting a "tap" (a third wire leading to an analyzer) can easily corrupt the signal because once the signal reaches the end of the branch/tap it will reflect back and recombine with the original signal, messing up what the display reads. ![signal-tap-reflection (2).png](/design-assets/images/4202055.webp) Finally, I will need to take the recorded initialization sequence and reproduce it with a microcontroller to control the display. So to recap, this has just become three sub-projects: - Writing firmware for the RP2350 to turn it into a logic analyzer - Must have a 100Mhz+ sample rate - Must have enough bandwidth to record the 150ms initialization sequence of the display - Must have at least 2 channels (one for each wire in data lane 0) - Creating an interposer circuit that delicately intercepts the signal between the phone and display without corrupting it - Must translate between the 1.2V logical voltage of the phone to the 3.3V logical voltage of the RP2350 analyzer - Creating a circuit that allows my microcontroller to send required 4-lane MIPI DSI to the display - Must allow 4Gbps to be converted into 1Gbps-per-lane MIPI DSI # RP2350 Logic Analyzer The big challenges in creating this were balancing the work done by the microcontroller with the work done by the host, and balancing the amount of information recorded with the amount of storage that information takes up. You will see that the final design has the RP2350 recording the minimum amount of information possible for the host computer to still be able to reconstruct the final result. For all intents and purposes, the host computer has infinite resources whereas the microcontroller has very limited resources. Reading through the RP2350 data sheet, I found so many amazing features and capabilities. The feature(s) that will be useful for this sub-project are PIO and DMA. ## Programmable IO Programmable IO (PIO) is an incredible peripheral of the RP2350. It contains 12 "state machines" which are extremely simple but **fast** mini-processors. The have only a pair of registers, and two additional shift registers. Their instruction set has just 10 instructions. The crucial part that makes these state machines invaluable in this project is their ability to run deterministically and with cycle-accurate timing. Every instruction is guaranteed to run in exactly 1 clock cycle. ## Direct Memory Access Direct Memory Access (DMA) is a peripheral that many microcontrollers have that can move data around the system without the involvement of the main processor. On the RP2350, it can move a single 32-bit word once per system clock cycle. At 150MHz, that is a bandwidth of 4.8 Gbps, but when overclocked to 250MHz, that is 8Gbps. ## First ideas There are already existing logic analyzer projects for the RP2350 that sample at the system clock speed, and record for a short duration (usually a couple thousand samples before and after a trigger). The idea is to use the following short PIO program: ```asm .out 32 left auto 32 ; configures auto-push .wrap_target ; wrap here when .wrap is reached in pins, 4 ; sample pins, repeats every cycle due to .wrap .wrap ; jump to wrap_target ``` This program samples from 4 GPIO pins every system cycle, and puts them in the Input Shift Register, which once full, pushes that 32-bit word to system memory via DMA. The system clock speed is by default 150MHz, and can even be safely overclocked to over 250MHz! Seems like we have our solution... right? Of course not. There is a problem with this design. The RP2350 has 512KB of memory, which can store a maximum of just 1 million samples at 100MHz. This comes out to just 0.01s, while the initialization sequence of the display can span more than 0.15s. There are two solutions to consider: - Find a way to move data from the chip to a host computer at a fast enough rate - Process the data on-chip to compress it ### Moving data off-chip The Raspberry Pi Pico 2 board has one micro-usb connection with a maximum bandwidth of 12Mbps. Our PIO program will be pulling in at least 400Mbps, so micro-usb is just not an option here. ### Processing the data on-chip Chances are, most of the time the wires will not be changing state from one sample to the next. We can therefore compress this data by only recording the transitions, or "edges". ![edge-compression-diagram.png](/design-assets/images/3662675.webp) Okay so great! Let's just use some code to monitor the stream of samples and every time the sampled value changes, we record an "event" that says something like "wire 1 change from low to high at 1250ns". Unfortunately, the main processor is not nearly fast enough to do this. The incoming data stream is overwhelming, at 4 bits per clock cycle, the main processor would have to compare a 4-bit `previous` state to the 4-bit `new` state, and possibly record an event, every single clock cycle. That is just not possible because the comparison and branching logic alone would consume multiple clock cycles. Even if we were somehow able to compare 7 samples at a time to their previous states with something like: ```c if ((x & 0x0FFFFFFF) ^ (x >> 4)) { ... } ``` The condition will take at least 4 cycles to evaluate, which leaves only 3 cycles for the body of the branch, and for jumping back to the top of the loop. It's really just not do-able atleast for someone of my skill. This dilemma made me think, what else is there on this chip that **could** process information at the required speed? Well, there are two cores on this chip but that won't help that much. There are however, still our 11 unused PIO State Machines. So my idea was to somehow figure out a way to use PIO machines to process the incoming data stream. ### Timing If a PIO machine is generating events, these events need a timestamp. PIO machines do not have direct access to system timers and clocks. Actually, either way the most accurate system clock available to the chip is only precise to 1 microsecond, orders of magnitude more than the time scales we are dealing with. However! Once again, PIO to the rescue. We can get PIO to keep its own time in the form of a sample counter. Since the PIO programs are cycle-accurate and deterministic, we can keep a cycle-accurate counter within a PIO machine. This does however add instructions to the loop and decrease our sample rate significantly. ### Sampling and Processing in the same place The first idea I considered was having the sampling state machine (SM0) compare states and generate events. However, this processing takes cycles and would drop the sample rate to once every 8-10 cycles, an order of magnitude slower. ### Sample then process The 2nd idea I had was streaming data from SM0 to a number of "processing" state machines where SM1 would handle the 4n-th sample, and SM2 the (4n+1)-th sample, etc. up to SM5. This of course has the problem that each machine needs the previous sample to compare to, but that sample was not sent to it because it was sent to the SM below it. It would need to be one state machine, but then we run into the same problem where one state machine would have to process a sample every cycle (impossible). ## The analyzer firmware I settled on a solution that allows a system-clock sample-rate (250MHz) while still keeping timing and processing within PIO. I came up with this solution by first putting everything I needed into one PIO program: - Sample - Increment Sample Count - Compare sample to previous sample - Possibly emit an event `[sample_count | new_state]` - set `prev_state = new_state` This program has a sample rate of 1/8th system-clock speed, as the main loop has 8 instructions along its path. I then stumbled upon another powerful feature of PIO: Multiple state machines can be started at the exact same time, and stay synchronized indefinitely. This sparked an idea: - Duplicate the 8-cycle PIO sampler program 8x - Start each machine with 8 different phases (+0 cycles, +1 cycles, ..., +7 cycles) This would give us 8 sampling machines, each sampling once every 8 cycles, but with their phases being slightly offset from each other such that exactly one machine samples the input each system cycle. Now we have 8 streams of events instead of 1... How in the world is that supposed to become one recording. Well, the information is all there, for each system cycle, **one of** the streams has the information of what the wire state was at that cycle. I wrote an algorithm to combine these 8 streams of edge events into a single stream. The idea is that for cycle `c`, the state of the wire is the state in the last recorded event of stream `c % 8`. Now, this processing could be done on the microprocessor, but I found it much simpler to write this algorithm in python on the host machine, rather than in C on the microprocessor. I did actually write a microprocessor version of the algorithm, but I found that it didn't hold up well under load and it starved the code that processed and sent the events over USB. The data is already compressed into events, we just need to store it and we can combine the streams later. ![four-phase-pio-sampling-bits-4x.png](/design-assets/images/2464686.webp) The PIO program I wrote to do this is as follows: ### The Sampling Program ```asm .program capture8 .pio_version 1 pull block ; per-SM offset from the TX FIFO out x, 32 phase: jmp x-- phase ; stagger this SM mov y, !null ; prev := all-ones so the first sample always emits mov osr, !null ; osr := 0xFFFFFFFF out null, 20 ; osr := 0x00000FFF (12-bit counter seed) jmp decrement .wrap_target event: ; x=value, osr=count (already decremented this sample) in osr, 12 ; ISR <- count in x, 4 ; ISR <- value (every second event hits 32 -> autopush) mov y, x ; prev := current value ; falls through to decrement decrement: mov x, osr ; x := count jmp x-- sample ; count non-zero -> sample; zero -> heartbeat below sample_heartbeat: ; heartbeat (count was 0, so x is now 0xFFFFFFFF) mov osr, x ; osr := 0xFFFFFFFF mov x, pins ; sample out null, 20 ; osr := 0x00000FFF (reseed) .wrap sample: mov osr, x ; store the decremented count (one tick per sample) mov x, pins ; sample jmp x!=y event ; change -> emit (y = prev, preserved) jmp decrement [2] ; --- PATHS --- ; with event: 8 cycles ; no event: 6 + [2] = 8 cycles ; underflow/heartbeat: 8 cycles | sample | 8 cycles ``` Now I faced a lot of challenges when designing this program and I'm going to talk about them, but feel free to skip to **The Interposer PCB** if it is not of interest to you. #### Register use The program has 2 general purpose registers (`x` and `y`) yet needs to keep track of **three** things: `prev_state`, `new_state`, and `sample_count`. There are two additional shift-registers, the OSR and ISR registers. ISR can be pushed to main memory, and OSR can pull from main memory (simplified). We cannot use ISR as we have it configured to automatically push to main memory once 32 bits are written to it. Thus, we store `sample_count` in OSR, and move data around between OSR, x and y, to operate on them as only x and y can be compared or decremented. Our register assignment is generally: - `x` -> `new_state` (the incoming sample) - `y` -> `prev_state` (the previous sample) - `osr` -> `sample_count` (inverse of the number of samples taken*) * Sort of... it's explained more in **Keeping Time** Data is moved around regularly, but that can only be done when one of the registers' values is no longer needed. Particularly, when `x` = `y`, i.e. when we've set prev_state to new_state, we no longer need new_state and can use `x` to move data around or swap values. #### Keeping time PIO Assembly does not have an add instruction, or even an increment instruction. The instruction of interest is actually `jmp x-- sample`, which jumps to a certain part of the program if the value of x is non-zero, and then **decrements** `x`. Thus our sample counter must work in reverse, starting at a high number and counting down. We actually encounter yet a 2nd problem when we consider that this counter has a limited size. Specifically, it can theoretically count down from a maximum of the 32-bit value **4,294,967,295**, which is about 34 seconds of sampling. This is actually enough, but it is not that simple. We have a maximum of 32 bits for each event we emit, so if we were to use 32 bits for timing, we have no bits left for the actual sample. The sample needs 4 bits for 4 channels, so we have 28 bits left for a sample count which brings our recording down to 2 seconds long. This will make it difficult to capture the Display Init Sequence as we will have to turn on the analyzer around the same time we turn the phone on. Additionally, 32-bit events take up a lot of space per-event. In fact, at maximum bandwidth, there would be a 32-bit event emitted every system cycle, saturating the DMA controller bandwidth completely (which is what takes the events from PIO and puts them into memory). This is risky because DMA competes with the processor for memory access, and a single moment of contention could cause DMA to overload and skip an event. In this architecture, skipping an event is actually catastrophic and means we need to restart the whole analyzer from scratch. Thus, we actually use 12-bit timing. So the sample counter is initially 0x00000FFF and counts to 0, then underflows to 0xFFFFFFFF and is shifted right to get 0x00000FFF again. This underflowing is actually also catastrophic, as two events might be captured with enough time between that the counter underflowed and ended up at the same number + 1. It would normally be impossible to distinguish whether the event happened 8 cycles later, or 32,768 cycles later, or 65,536 cycles later, and so on. To solve this problem, we add a "Heartbeat". We make it mandatory that each machine emit an event every time its sample counter underflows. This makes it possible to reconstruct the absolute sample number of an event. It does however reduce our analyzer bandwidth by a tiny amount as the machines together will emit 61,035 heartbeats per second even under no load. The benefit is that we can record for as long as we want. #### Keeping phase Why 8 copies and not 4? In order to keep the phase, every possible path from a sample instruction back to itself (every possible loop) must be exactly 8 instructions long. Some of the things the PIO program has to do take less than 8 instructions, so they must be padded (ex. `jmp decrement [2]` adds 2 cycles of doing nothing). Conversely, no operation can take more than 8 instructions and that forced me to need to come up with an interesting structure. I chose 8 copies because the shortest that I was able to make the sample -> event -> heartbeat path was 8 instructions. **Two sample instructions** To save on both space and instructions, the program actually has **two** spots where it samples the input (`mov x, pins`). There are not enough instructions in our 8-instruction budget to set `prev_state = new_state` **and** decrement `sample_count` **and** emit a heartbeat **and** reset `sample_count = 0x00000FFF` **and** return to the sample loop, so the program must sample once again in the middle of this path; using **where it is in the program** as part of the program state/memory. The upper sample instruction is part of a path that **definitely** emits an event, because `sample_count` will have underflowed during the previous sample. The lower sample instruction is the normal path where an event **might** be emitted if the wire state changed. ### Memory In order to record a long enough period at the expected 20 million events/s rate, I also wrote some firmware to utilize two 8MB PSRAM chips to store events. The PSRAM chips use QPI, but the RP2350's native QPI is inaccessible on the dev board, and the native SPI peripheral is far too slow at 75MHz. Instead, I wrote a PIO driver for the PSRAM chips that was able to achieve at 50MB/s (400Mbps) write speed detailed below: ```asm .wrap_target start: out x, 16 side 0 ; # output bytes (CE# high, CLK low) out y, 16 ; # input bytes mov pindirs, !null side 0 set pins, 0 side 0 [3] ; assert CE# with the original setup delay jmp x-- write write: out pins, 4 side 0 nop side 1 out pins, 4 side 0 write_condition: nop side 1 jmp x-- write jmp y-- start_wait_cycles side 0 jmp restart start_wait_cycles: mov pindirs, null side 1 [1] set x, 4 side 0 [1] wait_loop: nop side 1 [1] jmp x-- wait_loop side 0 [3] read: in pins, 4 side 1 [1] nop side 0 [3] in pins, 4 side 1 [1] read_condition: jmp y-- read side 0 [3] restart: nop [3] side 0 ; +16ns wait after last CLK edge (CE# still low) set pins, 1 side 0 ; deassert CE# irq 0 rel ; flag this state machine's transfer complete .wrap ``` With two chips bringing the write bandwidth up to 100MB/s, which is enough to sustain full load until the chips filled completely. This was done by first encoding events into the wire format, then storing these "blocks" in a queue, waiting to be sent out via USB. Once the queue's occupancy reaches a certain threshold, 256 byte chunks of it are paged out to PSRAM, while older chunks are left in the queue so the USB controller still has data to send. This actually didn't end up mattering as the display init sequence never stayed at its max edge rate for long enough to need the PSRAM buffer. # The interposer PCB Creating the interposer PCB was a challenge for me because I had to learn a lot about electrical signals and how they behave at high frequencies. The problem is that I need to tap the D0 pair, which is a high-speed differential pair while in HS mode. It the tap distorts the signal too much, the display will not work and the phone may even crash. ## The Tap A resistor can isolate the rest of the circuit from the tapped line. Higher value resistors will isolate more strongly, but at the same time, the signal will have a harder time getting through a high-value resistor. Specifically the "rise time" increases with both the resistance value and the capacitance of the line after the resistor. The rise time is roughly the time it takes for the voltage to change from high to low or low to high. The resistor also needs to be as close to the tapped line as possible because the resistor itself is a change in impedance and **will** reflect the signal. If the resistor is close to the line though, the reflected wave will still be roughly in-phase with the original signal. In the extreme case, an infinity-ohm resistor that is right on the tapped line reflects the signal perfectly in-phase with the original signal, the same as no reflection at all. This isn't really practical though. With a 1 kilo-ohm resistor, and a few millimeters of copper trace (~2pf capacitance), the rise time of the trace after the resistor will be under 10ns. Since our LP signal edges are 50ns apart, this will do. This resistance-capacitance pair also acts as a filter for the HS traffic. It forms what is called a low-pass RC filter, meaning lower frequency signals pass, and higher frequency signals are blocked/degraded. The increased rise-time filters out signals faster than 100MHz, so HS traffic will not show up on our analyzer. The analyzer input is the next stop for the signal, and in our case it is a GPIO pin on our RP2350. This input is very high impedance, close to just an open circuit, so it will reflect our signal right back towards the resistor. Luckily, the resistor prevents (much of) this reflection from reaching the original signal line. ## Voltage conversion Except this is not actually all we need. We cannot just connect it straight to the analyzer because the voltage range of the signal in LP mode is 0.0-1.2V whereas the RP2350 recognizes 0.0-3.3V. A logical `1` in the signal would be 1.2V and would probably be interpreted as a `0` by the RP2350 which is expecting 3.3V for a `1`. To do this, I decided to use comparators, because I am new to this and did not know that logic-level translator ICs existed. Anyways, my idea was to use a comparator per signal with a threshold of 0.6V. A voltage over 0.6V will be turned into 3.3V and below will be turned into 0.0V. The comparator inputs are also high-impedance, so the output of the comparator is completely isolated from the input. The input does reflect the signal, but I can place it much closer to the resistor than I can place the RP2350, so this actually benefits us. To create this 0.6V, I am using this voltage divider: This works because it places the reference voltage line in the middle between 3.3V and Ground. The total resistance between 3.3V and Ground is 2,200 Ω, and the reference voltage is in the middle, about (400 Ω / 2,200 Ω) = 18.2% of the way between 0.0V and 3.3V. So the voltage in the middle, should be (18.2%) * (3.3V) ≈ 0.6V. ## HDMI output Just in case the PSRAM chips were not enough, I added an HDMI output hooked up to 8 of the free GPIO pins on the RP2350. The chip has a peripheral called HSTX (High-Speed Transfer) that can be programmed to act as an HDMI output. The idea is to send data out of HSTX at nearly 1Gbps. This would be complicated to do but it's worth going through the pain of designing it because if I need it I definitely do not want to have to order a new PCB. ## Other PCB elements There is also another voltage divider that divides PP_VDD_MAIN_HILO (from the display connector) by two. This voltage I believe to come straight from the battery so I wanted to input this into an ADC on the RP2350 to confirm this. The final PCB design is this: The two headers are spaced such that the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 board can plug right into it and sit on top of this board. There is a plug on the bottom and receptacle on top. The plug goes to iPhone and the receptacle goes to the display. They are wired together, with MIPI_D0_P and MIPI_D0_N along with MIPI_CLK_P/N tapped and routed to the comparators. The final setup will look like this: # Interception Results I received the board, did some electrical checks, realized the voltage divider was wrong, fixed it, and then finally tried it out. The results came in, and I had successfully captured loads of interesting-looking activity. Upon further inspection, I could clearly see the initialization, the MIPI LP DCS commands, and even the individual frames being sent on a 16.67ms period (60Hz). This is the first thing I saw: At first glance, I can see that... *something* is definitely happening. I'd need to zoom in quite a bit to see what. Here we see there is a ~120ms initialization period, followed by spikes of activity on a 16.67ms period, consistent with 60Hz video mode. Zooming into one of the spikes on the right half... We see that each spike is actually a burst of 154 sub-spikes over a span of exactly 0.997 ms. There is also some additional activity roughly in the center. If we zoom into that... We see that this is in fact a DCS command being sent. Specifically this is the "Display On" command. Interestingly, this is actually the 4th frame sent by the phone. The display image is not made visible until the 4th frame, likely to prevent flickering and ensure stability before visible operation. The other spikes, or rather the other **dips** are entrances into HS mode, characterized by the green line going low, followed by the pink line going low. The line exits HS mode when both lines are pulled high again. This actually means the frames are sent in between these spikes, not during them. The many dips we see within the spikes are likely vertical blanking rows with the ones before the DCS command being the vertical front porch and the remaining being the back porch. In the init sequence, we see there are two bursts of commands sent at t=16ms and t=25ms. Inspecting these bursts, we see that the first one is the DCS "Exit Sleep" command while the second one is the sequence: - Set Max Return Size 32 bytes - Read Device ID - Device ID Response Those last two I infer from the fact that the response does not change between startups, but actually **does** change if I swap the display for an alternate display. After the initialization, it drops straight into video mode and starts sending frames. There are a few DCS commands sent within the first couple frames. - In the 1st frame, brightness control is enabled - In the 4th frame, the display is made visible - In the 6th frame, the brightness is set to 0x02E4, likely 720/1023 = 70% brightness I also captured a period where I was changing the brightness on the phone, resulting in many many DCS generic long writes to register 0x51. Which is what led me to figuring out what command was setting the brightness. Now, within the 154 spikes that make up that burst in-between frames, the period of those spikes is about 6.44us. Since 6.44us * (2436 + 154) = 16689us = 16.68ms, this is pretty good evidence that the row-period is 6.44us. The row-period is the time taken to send one row of the screen along with all the synchronization and timing packets needed for that row. So we know: - The vertical blanking front and back porch - The vertical blanking period (997us) - All LP DCS commands that are sent - The timing and wire state during initialization We still do not know: - The pixel clock rate - Whether the display is operated in burst mode, non-burst with sync events, or non-burst with sync pulses. - If any other DCS commands are sent in HS mode. - The amount of horizontal blanking. We can deduce that the pixel clock rate must be at least 1 Gbps.

title: Belfort Events
brief: An event and ticketing platform built for my cousin's night club.
description:
This website, made with Kotlin, PostgreSQL, React and Stripe is a ticketing platform for my cousin's nightclub (Belfort). It allows users to purchase tickets to Belfort and for staff to scan tickets at the door. The platform provides various analytics and promo code options.

The platform supports the thousands of students that attend Belfort each week.

title: KAsyncWorld
brief: This is a library I made for usage in minecraft plugins. It allows plugins to create in-memory worlds, and modify worlds asynchronously and in parallel at a billion edits per second.
description:
https://github.com/ultragrav/KAsyncWorld

## Purpose
The purpose of this project is to provide a representation of a minecraft world that can be modified and processed asynchronously and off of the main server thread. Furthermore it is intended to provide a way to edit large parts of the world blazingly fast, and without causing lag. I also needed this project to provide an API for creating in-memory worlds, which are worlds in the game that are not backed
by any files or folders on the host machine, but are stored completely in-memory and are volatile, leaving no trace behind after unloading. This project provides such an API and also provides a custom
codec and format to serialize and deserialize these in-memory worlds in milliseconds, ensuring quick saving and loading functionality.

## Problem
The Minecraft Server application is only single-threaded and cannot make use of multi-core systems. An annoying result of this is that none of Minecraft's internal world structures are thread-safe and there are many side effects of doing block processing.

## Solution
This project provides an external api that is per-chunk thread-safe and can be handled entirely outside the main server thread. When changes are finished, a number of optimizations allow for the changes to be pushed to the real world extremely quickly and with only a single function call. Chunks must be written back to the real world on the main thread, but write-back is so optimized that speeds may reach up to a billion blocks per second in some cases. This is a tremendous improvement over standard Spigot APIs which grant the user speeds of less than a million blocks per second.

## Features
- Asynchronous manipulation of worlds
- Fast write-back to real world (~500 million blocks/sec on MidnightSky servers)
- In-memory world creation and handling
- Blazingly fast custom world codec for in-memory worlds
- Sub-second load time for 16,000 chunk in-memory world

## Timings
Here are some in-game tests done to measure the speed of saving/replacing/restoring a region of ~8 million blocks.

![Screenshot 2025-06-02 at 7.07.28 PM.png](/design-assets/images/1405918.webp)

As you can see, both read and write speeds may exceed **1 billion** blocks / second, which is over 1000x faster than through the Spigot API and even exceeds the speeds of the FastAsyncWorldEdit plugin.


## Usage
Let's start with some examples first.
This is a snippet from the source code of MidnightSky (some parts omitted for brevity)
```kotlin
val world = adv.map.world
val aw = AW.createAsyncWorld(world, AsyncWorld.EditType.SPARSE)

val sc = ..
val pasteAt = ..
Schematics.paste(sc, aw, pasteAt.x, pasteAt.y, pasteAt.z)

box = ..

// Kick out the people inside
..

aw.syncFlush()
```

This is another snippet from MidnightSky
```kotlin
fun destroyPrepStation() {
    val poi = map.data.poiList.first { it.type == WarMapPoiType.PREP_STATION }

    val dims = ..
    val x = poi.x.toInt() - dims.x / 2
    val y = poi.y.toInt() - 1
    val z = poi.z.toInt() - dims.z / 2

    val aw = AW.createAsyncWorld(world.bukkitWorld, AsyncWorld.EditType.SPARSE)
    val corner1 = Vec3i(x, y, z)
    val corner2 = corner1 + dims
    val box = corner1 box corner2

    aw.setBox(box, Material.AIR.createBlockData())
    aw.flush()
}
```

As you can see it is extremely simple to use. You might notice that aw.syncFlush() is used in the first snippet yet aw.flush() in the following one. The difference is that aw.flush() adds the changes to a queue
 that will ~eventually write the changes back to the real world (usually quite fast), and returns immediately. The queue will possibly spread the write-back over multiple game ticks so as to avoid lagging the server thread. syncFlush() also adds the edits to the queue, however it guarantees that the edits are written back completely before it returns, and if it is called from the main thread, it will start immediately and will not return until completely finished, no tick spreading is done.

 The following snippet shows how you can create an in-memory world.

 ```kotlin
customWorld = AW.inMemoryWorldProvider.createWorld(
    "island-$croppedIslandIdStr-${type.name.lowercase()}",
    InMemoryWorldOptions(
        0 until type.size,
        0 until type.size,
        worldEnv,
        codec = AW.compressedCodec
    ),
    currentSave
)
```

Where currentSave is of type PackedWorld and can be obtained as such:
```kotlin
customWorld.unload(true) // true for save
currentSave = customWorld.saveAndPack()
```

saveAndPack() can also be called while the world is loaded. It is unloaded first in this case to avoid any modifications to the world being missed before it is unloaded.

## How it works
AsyncWorld objects comprise of a map of AsyncChunk objects, each of which contain AsyncChunkSection objects which store the real changes. 

### Write-back
All AsyncChunk objects can be written back to the world in the write-back process through the use of a ChunkIO class. A default one is provided in the AW.chunkIO global.
- Blocks are transferred from AsyncChunkSection to Minecraft Chunk Section while still compressed to maximize transfer speed.
- There are numerous other optimizations in the chunk write process that I will not cover here.
- When multiple chunks must be written back from a single AsyncWorld on a multi-core system, KAsyncWorld will write multiple chunks in parallel by multi-threading the writing of non-overlapping chunk edits.
- Write-back speeds are fast, usually **0.25-0.5ms** per chunk during normal operation.

### AsyncChunkSection
- Blocks are stored compressed, taking up as little as 4 bits per block and depending on the number of unique block types in a section (16x16x16 cube).
- The block information is stored in the exact format Minecraft internally stores blocks, this is done intentionally to make write-back as fast as possible.
- Sections not only track what blocks they are comprised of but also what blocks were actually changed
- Sections can be iterated over and will only iterate over the blocks that have actually been modified. Depending on the type of section,
this may default to every block, but for most types (like what is given to you when you use EditType.SPARSE), the iteration order will be in the order the blocks were modified and furthermore only cover
modified blocks, as the changes are tracked (in one of three ways depending on usage).

#### LinkedIterationStrategy
When you modify a block in an AsyncWorld that supports change tracking using Linked Iteration (most of them), if the block you changed has not already been modified, it will be linked into a 4096-entry array that acts
as space for a linked list. When iterating over the modified section, the iterator will walk this linked list, covering the modified blocks in the order they were modified. This strategy
is the default because it is the most performant in the average case. It is very quick for write-back as only changed blocks are iterated over and there is no seek time for finding the next
changed block as there is with Flag Iteration which we will cover below.

#### FlagIterationStrategy
When using Flag Iteration, iteration is not ordered, and the changes are tracked using a bitmap of size 4096, stored as 64 longs. No guarantees are made on the iteration order, but only modified blocks
will be iterated over. This strategy uses less memory than Linked Iteration but is often less performant in write-back because the whole bitmap must be iterated over.

#### NormalIterationStrategy
This is the simplest, iteration covers every block, modified or not, in a predictable order.

It should be noted that each section also stores how many of its blocks are dirty (changed) and also how many of each type of block it contains (modified or not).

### Optimizations

- In the case that a section is completely dirty (4096 modified blocks) then write-back can be sped up by just transferring the whole data array to the minecraft chunk section instead of picking out individual blocks. This is a big part of the speed up KAsyncWorld provides as usually the data array will only be 256 64-bit longs (16 blocks per long).
- In the case that a section is completely air, and also completely dirty, then a further optimization can be made by just deleting that section from the world entirely.

### Caveats
To transfer the data array directly to a minecraft chunk section, the compression encoding (block palette) needs to match, if they do not, the palette must be replaced. Luckily, palettes are quite small compared to the data storage, so this is quite fast.

### In-Memory Worlds
- In-memory worlds are created quickly by skipping much of the setup that Minecraft usually performs, on the basis that much of it is unneeded and irrelevant for worlds used by projects that this library
is meant to serve
- There is no chunk generation by default in these worlds.
- Chunks that are not in use by the Minecraft internals are cached in an encoded format (and potentially compressed) to save memory.
- Chunk loading by Minecraft internals is extremely fast as the chunks need not be loaded from disk, and are instead quickly uncompressed and decoded from memory.
- The chunk codec can be customized but a compact and fast implementation is provided as AW.compressedCodec.

### Fun Fact
While writing here about one of the optimizations I had implemented, I discovered I never actually finished implementing that optimization. I finished it, and it increased write-back speed by 300%.
